meaning_en: to make something happen
scene: {A} wishes the rain would stop. {B} does a ridiculous dance with a paper umbrella, and the sun comes out.
bubble: {B}'s silly dance brought about a miracle!
example: The new school rules brought about a big change in our classroom.

options: The new school rules brought about a big change in our classroom.
Please bring about the library book back to me tomorrow.
She brought about her lunch in a small blue box.
practice.why: Bring about means to make something happen, usually a change or a result.

meaning_en: to break into pieces, or stop working
scene: {A} proudly carries a huge sandcastle. Suddenly it falls into tiny pieces on {A}'s shoes.
bubble: Oh no! My masterpiece came apart!
example: The old toy came apart when the little boy dropped it.

options: The old toy came apart when the little boy dropped it.
The teacher came apart to see our drawings on the wall.
My cousin came apart for dinner at our house on Sunday.
practice.why: Come apart means to break into pieces, so the toy breaking is the correct use.

meaning_en: to accept what happens without fighting it
scene: {A} floats down a river on a tiny rubber duck. {B} sits calmly on the duck's head, smiling.
bubble: {B} just goes with the flow!
example: Our plans changed, so we decided to go with the flow.

options: He went with the flow and shouted at everyone to change the plan.
She always goes with the flow, so she plans every minute of the trip.
Our plans changed, so we decided to go with the flow.
practice.why: Go with the flow means accepting what happens calmly, not arguing or fighting.

text: like a bat out of hell
meaning_en: extremely fast
meaning_es: como alma que lleva el diablo
scene: {A} sees a snail overtaking a bicycle. {B} zooms past both on a skateboard with flaming sneakers.
bubble: {B} is going like a bat out of hell!
example: When the bell rang, the children ran out like a bat out of hell.

options: When the bell rang, the children ran out like a bat out of hell.
The old man strolled like a bat out of hell along the beach.
The snail crawled like a bat out of hell across the path.
practice.why: Like a bat out of hell means extremely fast, so only the running children fit.

meaning_en: to be mentioned or to happen unexpectedly
scene: {A} gives a serious speech when a pigeon walks onto the stage and starts to sing.
bubble: Well, that didn't come up in rehearsal!
example: A problem came up at work, so Dad came home late.

options: A problem came up at work, so Dad came home late.
My phone battery came up, so I put it in the drawer.
We came up a good idea for the school project.
practice.why: Come up means to happen unexpectedly or to be mentioned in a conversation.

meaning_en: to do something slowly, without hurrying
scene: {A} sprints to every class. {B} walks very slowly with a cup of tea and a big smile.
bubble: "Take your time," says {B}, calmly.
example: Take your time with the test; there is no need to hurry.

options: Take your time or you will miss the bus; hurry!
Take your time with the test; there is no need to hurry.
Take your time to hurry; the film starts in two minutes.
practice.why: Take your time means do it slowly, without hurrying, so it cannot go with running.

meaning_en: the health of a whole population, seen as one thing
scene: {A} washes hands with a giant bar of soap, while {B} sprays a whole town with bubbles.
bubble: {B} is a public health hero!
example: The school started a campaign to improve public health.

options: The mayor opened a new public health where people can swim.
The school started a campaign to improve public health.
Public health means how healthy one single person feels today.
practice.why: Public health is about keeping a whole population healthy, not a person or an object.

meaning_en: to be the person who decides
scene: {A} wears a paper crown and points at everyone. The cat sits on the real throne, looking bored.
bubble: {A} calls the shots... or maybe the cat does!
example: The captain calls the shots, so listen to her instructions.

options: The captain calls the shots, so listen to her instructions.
He called the shots from the park to say he was late.
The substitute teacher calls the shots, so she follows everyone's ideas.
practice.why: Call the shots means to be the one who decides, like a captain or a boss.

meaning_en: to stop a fire or a cigarette burning
scene: {A} blows a small birthday candle. A giant fire hose suddenly appears behind {B}.
bubble: {B} brought the biggest fire hose!
example: The firefighters put out the fire in only ten minutes.

options: The children put out a candle by lighting it with a match.
The firefighters put out the fire in only ten minutes.
The firefighters put out a big fire by pouring petrol on it.
practice.why: Put out means to stop a fire or a cigarette burning.

meaning_en: to take control of something
scene: {A} sits in the captain's chair. A tiny dog jumps in and takes over the whole spaceship.
bubble: The dog has taken over!
example: Maria took over the club when the old president left.

options: She took over the book from the shelf and read it.
I took over my coat because it was cold outside.
Maria took over the club when the old president left.
practice.why: Take over means to take control of something that someone else had.

meaning_en: to start suddenly, said of war, fire or disease
scene: {A} is at a picnic when a flock of ducks starts a loud food fight over sandwiches.
bubble: A duck war broke out!
example: A fire broke out in the kitchen, but nobody was hurt.

options: The glass broke out into two pieces when it fell.
A fire broke out in the kitchen, but nobody was hurt.
He broke out his leg when he fell off the bicycle.
practice.why: Break out is used for wars, fires or diseases that start suddenly. A broken window is different.

meaning_en: to say something that upsets somebody by accident
scene: {A} tells {B}, "I love your haircut!" Then {B} turns around, wearing a very obvious wig.
bubble: Oops! {A} put their foot in it!
example: I put my foot in it when I asked her about the party she wasn't invited to.

options: He put his foot in it by giving a very kind and perfect speech.
I put my foot in it so I could stand on the chair.
I put my foot in it when I asked her about the party she wasn't invited to.
practice.why: Put your foot in it means to say something that upsets someone by accident.

meaning_en: a friendly greeting to somebody you have not met for a while
scene: {A} meets {B} at the supermarket after three years. They hug in the middle of the cereal aisle.
bubble: "Long time no see!" shouts {A}.
example: Long time no see! How was your summer?

options: We said 'Long time no see' to a friend we had met yesterday.
Long time no see! How was your summer?
At the end of the party, we waved and shouted, 'Long time no see!'
practice.why: Long time no see is a friendly greeting for someone you have not met for a while.

meaning_en: to make somebody else take the responsibility
meaning_es: pasar la pelota, no asumir la responsabilidad
scene: {A} holds a hot potato and throws it quickly to {B}. {B} throws it to the dog.
bubble: Nobody wants it. They're passing the buck!
example: The manager passed the buck instead of fixing the problem.

options: The manager passed the buck instead of fixing the problem.
She passed the buck and told everyone, 'It was my mistake.'
I passed the buck by doing all the work on my own.
practice.why: Pass the buck means to make someone else take responsibility for a problem.

meaning_en: to give something to somebody without asking for money
scene: {A} stands in the street with a sign: "Free hugs and free socks." {B} runs away with ten socks.
bubble: {A} is giving away everything!
example: The bakery gives away free bread at the end of the day.

options: The shop gave away cheap sweets for fifty pence each.
The bakery gives away free bread at the end of the day.
My teacher gave away my homework back with a good mark.
practice.why: Give away means to give something without asking for money, so free bread fits.

meaning_en: the spring that is coming
scene: {A} puts a calendar on the fridge and circles "next spring" with a huge heart. A flower waves from the window.
bubble: Next spring can't come soon enough!
example: We are going to visit my grandparents next spring.

options: Last week was the next spring of my life.
We are going to visit my grandparents next spring.
Yesterday I planted these seeds, and they grew next spring.
practice.why: Next spring means the spring that is coming, so it names a future time.

meaning_en: better than all the others
scene: {A} bakes a cake. A judge tastes it and holds up a sign that says "Number 1" upside down.
bubble: {A}'s cakes are second to none!
example: Her singing is second to none in our school.

options: Our team is second to none, so we're the worst in town.
He came second to none in the race, so he didn't win.
Her singing is second to none in our school.
practice.why: Second to none means better than all the others.

meaning_en: fresh energy, or a fresh start for somebody or something
meaning_es: un nuevo aire, un impulso renovado
scene: {A} owns an old, rusty bicycle. {B} paints it gold, adds a bell and a flag, and the bike flies.
bubble: The bike got a new lease of life!
example: After the holiday, my grandfather had a new lease of life.

options: He felt a new lease of life, so he went to bed very sad and tired.
She signed a new lease of life to rent the flat.
After the holiday, my grandfather had a new lease of life.
practice.why: A new lease of life means fresh energy or a fresh start.

meaning_en: to use something so much that it can no longer be used
scene: {A} wears the same pair of sneakers every day. One day, both soles fall off at the bus stop.
bubble: Those sneakers are completely worn out!
example: My old backpack is worn out, so I need a new one.

options: My old backpack is worn out, so I need a new one.
She wore out her new dress to the party tonight.
I wore out the old jacket because it's still brand new and perfect.
practice.why: Wear out means that something has been used so much that it can't be used anymore.

meaning_en: completely unexpectedly
scene: {A} reads quietly in the garden. A man in a banana costume jumps out and sings "Happy birthday!"
bubble: It came out of the blue!
example: The invitation came out of the blue, so I wasn't ready.

options: The invitation came out of the blue, so I wasn't ready.
We planned the trip out of the blue for months.
He knew about the test out of the blue because the teacher told us a week ago.
practice.why: Out of the blue means completely unexpected, so a party planned for weeks cannot be out of the blue.

meaning_en: to cut off a piece with the teeth
scene: {A} bites off a huge piece of a sandwich. The sandwich is longer than a bus, and {B} just watches.
bubble: {A} bit off more than expected!
example: The dog bit off a piece of my sandwich when I wasn't looking.

options: The little girl bit off the light before she went to bed.
The dog bit off a piece of my sandwich when I wasn't looking.
I bit off the TV because the programme was boring.
practice.why: Bite off means to cut off a piece with the teeth, like a dog with a sandwich.

meaning_en: to take something out of a place with your hand
scene: {A} pulls and pulls a carrot out of the ground. A huge rabbit appears, holding the other end.
bubble: {A} pulled out a giant surprise!
example: He pulled out a tooth that was very loose.

options: She pulled out the door by pushing it with both hands.
He pulled out a tooth that was very loose.
We pulled out the picture to the wall with a nail.
practice.why: Pull out means to take something out of a place by hand.

meaning_en: to enter a sale on a cash register
scene: {A} works at a till with a long queue. {B} scans a watermelon, a chair and a tiny hippo.
bubble: "Ring up everything!" shouts {B}.
example: The shop assistant rang up my milk and bread together.

options: The cashier rang up a bell to wake the customers.
The teacher rang up the answers on the board with a red pen.
The shop assistant rang up my milk and bread together.
practice.why: Ring up means to enter a sale on a cash register.

meaning_en: to worry about something bad that cannot be changed
meaning_es: lamentarse por lo que ya no tiene remedio
scene: {A} cries beside a puddle of orange juice on the floor. {B} brings a mop and a tissue.
bubble: "Don't cry over spilt milk," says {B}.
example: It's just a broken cup. Don't cry over spilt milk.

options: It's just a broken cup. Don't cry over spilt milk.
She cried over spilt milk because her team won the cup.
Don't cry over spilt milk: you can still fix it before the deadline.
practice.why: Cry over spilt milk means worrying about something bad that cannot be changed.

meaning_en: to return something, or to make somebody remember
scene: {A} finds an old toy in a box. A big cloud of memories flies out as a swarm of balloons.
bubble: That song brings back so many memories!
example: Please bring back my book by Friday.

options: We brought back the dog for a walk to the park.
Bring back your umbrella to the picnic in case it rains.
Please bring back my book by Friday.
practice.why: Bring back can mean return something or make you remember something.

meaning_en: to give the main points briefly
scene: {A} tries to explain a long film in ten seconds. {B} holds up a card: "Dog meets cat, they dance."
bubble: Can you sum up the story, {A}?
example: At the end, the teacher summed up the lesson in three points.

options: He summed up the stairs because he was in a hurry.
She summed up her friends to invite them to the party.
At the end, the teacher summed up the lesson in three points.
practice.why: Sum up means to give the main points briefly.

meaning_en: uncertain, and it could still go wrong
scene: {A} balances on a rope over a pool. {B} cheers, holding a rubber duck in each hand.
bubble: It's touch and go. Who will fall in?
example: After the accident, it was touch and go for a few hours.

options: The test was touch and go, so everyone passed easily with full marks.
After the accident, it was touch and go for a few hours.
We played touch and go on the beach with a ball.
practice.why: Touch and go means uncertain, with a risk that things could end badly.

text: off the top of my head
meaning_en: from memory, without checking
scene: {A} is asked, "How many stars are there?" and answers instantly. {B} blinks in disbelief.
bubble: {A} knows it off the top of their head!
example: I don't know exactly, but off the top of my head it's about twenty.

options: I don't know exactly, but off the top of my head it's about twenty.
She checked every page carefully, and then answered off the top of her head.
I read the answer from the book off the top of my head.
practice.why: Off the top of my head means from memory, without checking.

meaning_en: to lift something, or to collect somebody
scene: {A} lifts a tiny puppy from the floor. {B} arrives with a big car to pick up the puppy and the dog bowl.
bubble: {B} came to pick up the whole zoo!
example: Can you pick up your sister from school at four?

options: Can you pick up your sister from school at four?
I'll pick up a good question on page ten for the exam.
She picked up her seat when the teacher came in.
practice.why: Pick up means to lift something or to collect someone, for example from school.

meaning_en: to finish a supply of something
scene: {A} looks at an empty box of cookies. {B} has chocolate on their face and a guilty smile.
bubble: Who used up all the cookies?
example: We used up all the paper, so we need to buy more.

options: I used up the computer for an hour and then turned it off.
We used up all the paper, so we need to buy more.
She used up her pen to write the invitations, and it's still new.
practice.why: Use up means to finish a supply, so nothing is left.

text: hit the nail on the head
meaning_en: to say exactly the right thing
scene: {A} throws a dart. It lands exactly in the middle of the board. {B} nods, wearing sunglasses.
bubble: "You hit the nail on the head!" cheers {B}.
example: You hit the nail on the head: that's exactly the problem.

options: You hit the nail on the head: that's exactly the problem.
He hit the nail on the head and got everything completely wrong.
She hit the nail on the head by saying nothing at all.
practice.why: Hit the nail on the head means to say exactly the right thing.

meaning_en: to come to somebody's home for a short visit
scene: {A} is eating alone. Then {B}, with five friends and a giant pizza, comes over to join.
bubble: Come over on Saturday and bring your games!
example: My cousin came over to watch the match at our house.

options: Our teacher came over to the cinema with us last Saturday.
My cousin came over to watch the match at our house.
The film came over at the cinema last week.
practice.why: Come over means to come to someone's home for a short visit.

meaning_en: to give permission for something to start
scene: {A} waves a green flag at a snail on a starting line. The snail doesn't move.
bubble: {A} gave the green light.
example: The teacher gave the green light for our science project.

options: The manager gave the green light and told us we couldn't do the project.
The teacher gave the green light for our science project.
She gave the green light to her plants with some water.
practice.why: Give the green light means to give permission for something to start.

meaning_en: something bad that happened and no longer matters
scene: {A} and {B} argued about a pizza last year. Now they share a big one under a tiny bridge.
bubble: "That's water under the bridge," says {A}.
example: We argued last year, but it's water under the bridge now.

options: We argued last year, but it's water under the bridge now.
The argument from this morning is water under the bridge, and we still shout.
I'm worried about next week's test because it's water under the bridge.
practice.why: Water under the bridge is something that happened and no longer matters.

meaning_en: impossible, not even worth discussing
scene: {A} asks a dragon for a lift to school. {B} holds up a "NO WAY" sign.
bubble: Dragon lifts are out of the question!
example: Going out alone at midnight is out of the question.

options: Going out alone at midnight is out of the question.
Staying for dessert is out of the question, so please give me a big slice.
A pizza for dinner is out of the question; I love it and we're having it tonight.
practice.why: Out of the question means impossible, not worth discussing.

meaning_en: in private, where the public cannot see
scene: {A} and {B} whisper in a closet full of coats. A cat listens at the door.
bubble: Plans are made behind closed doors.
example: The two leaders talked behind closed doors for hours.

options: The shop is behind closed doors, so everybody can see inside.
The news was shared behind closed doors on a big public stage.
The two leaders talked behind closed doors for hours.
practice.why: Behind closed doors means in private, where nobody else can see or hear.

text: come down to earth with a bump
meaning_en: to return suddenly to ordinary reality after a happy time
scene: {A} floats on a cloud of ice cream. Then the cloud pops, and {A} lands on a pile of homework.
bubble: Down to earth with a bump!
example: After the great holiday, I came down to earth with a bump on Monday.

options: I came down to earth with a bump when I won the first prize.
After the great holiday, I came down to earth with a bump on Monday.
He came down to earth with a bump and felt wonderful and relaxed.
practice.why: Come down to earth with a bump means to return suddenly to ordinary reality.

meaning_en: to take action to solve a problem or handle a situation
scene: {A} faces a mountain of dirty plates. {B} wears rubber gloves and a hero's cape.
bubble: {B} will deal with it!
example: We need to deal with this problem before the exam.

options: We need to deal with this problem before the exam.
The restaurant deals with traditional food: you can eat there.
They dealt with the shop in the town centre for ten euros.
practice.why: Deal with means to take action to solve a problem.

meaning_en: to lie down or extend your body fully
scene: {A} lies on the sofa like a starfish. {B} sits on the arm and sighs loudly.
bubble: "Stretch out and relax," says {B}.
example: After the long trip, he stretched out on the sofa.

options: The rubber band stretched out into a hundred pieces.
After the long trip, he stretched out on the sofa.
We stretched out the room with a bright yellow paint.
practice.why: Stretch out means to lie down or extend your body fully.

meaning_en: to increase gradually
scene: {A} adds one block at a time to a tower. Soon it is taller than the house, and {B} faints.
bubble: Tension is building up!
example: The noise built up until the teacher asked us to stop.

options: Heavy traffic builds up on the bridge, so the road is empty.
The noise built up until the teacher asked us to stop.
The workers built up the old bridge by taking it down.
practice.why: Build up means to increase gradually, so noise growing slowly fits.

meaning_en: in trouble with somebody
scene: {A} stands in front of an angry teacher, wearing a pot of paint on their head.
bubble: {A} is in hot water!
example: I'm in hot water because I forgot my mum's birthday.

options: I'm in hot water because I forgot my mum's birthday.
He is in hot water because he got the top mark in class.
We were in hot water, so we made a cup of tea.
practice.why: In hot water means in trouble with someone.

meaning_en: to stop a person or thing from rising or growing
scene: {A} sits on a balloon to keep it down. {B} laughs as it pops loudly.
bubble: You can't keep the noise down for long!
example: The teacher asked the children to keep their voices down.

options: Please keep down the radio so we can dance louder.
Keep down the gate open for the guests, please.
The teacher asked the children to keep their voices down.
practice.why: Keep down means to stop something rising or growing; voices must stay low.

meaning_en: to build or fix something in a high position
scene: {A} stands on a ladder and puts up a poster with a big smile. {B} holds the ladder and a cat.
bubble: {A} puts up posters for the talent show.
example: We put up a tent beside the lake last summer.

options: We put up a tent beside the lake last summer.
I put up my shoes before going to bed.
They put up the rubbish in the bin.
practice.why: Put up means to build or fix something in a high position, such as a tent or poster.

meaning_en: to learn a fact you did not know
scene: {A} finds a mysterious letter in the cereal box. {B} reads it with a magnifying glass.
bubble: Let's find out who sent it!
example: I want to find out what time the match starts.

options: I want to find out what time the match starts.
I found out my keys in the pocket of my coat.
He found out his glasses under the sofa.
practice.why: Find out means to learn a fact you did not know before.

meaning_en: abilities that you use to do things with your hands
scene: {A} fixes a bicycle while {B} bakes a cake. The cat sews a tiny hat for the dog.
bubble: They have lots of practical skills!
example: Learning practical skills like cooking is great for teenagers.

options: Practical skills are only the things you learn by reading in a book.
Learning practical skills like cooking is great for teenagers.
She has practical skills because she is rich and has a big house.
practice.why: Practical skills are abilities used to do things with your hands, like cooking.

meaning_en: to go, or to make something go, more slowly
scene: {A} runs on a treadmill in slow motion. {B} presses the button and the machine slows down.
bubble: Slow down, you're going too fast!
example: Slow down, please. The road is wet.

options: Slow down, please: we need to arrive five minutes earlier.
Slow down, please. The road is wet.
He slowed down his speed and drove faster.
practice.why: Slow down means to go, or make something go, more slowly.

meaning_en: the best point in time to do something
scene: {A} holds a cream pie. {B} is about to open a door. {A} waits, smiling, for the perfect second.
bubble: {A} is waiting for the right moment!
example: Wait for the right moment to ask your teacher a favour.

options: Wait for the right moment to ask your teacher a favour.
She chose the right moment to interrupt, so everyone was angry.
The right moment means any place where you can buy a cheap ticket.
practice.why: Right moment means the best point in time to do something.

meaning_en: to stop a supply, or to separate something by cutting
scene: {A} cuts off a long piece of spaghetti. {B}, at the other end, shouts as the plate falls.
bubble: Whoops! The power is cut off too!
example: The storm cut off the electricity for three hours.

options: The storm cut off the electricity for three hours.
The company cut off our water because we paid the bill early.
The film was cut off when the electricity came back on.
practice.why: Cut off means to stop a supply, like electricity, or to separate something.

meaning_en: to allow a person or an animal to leave a place
scene: {A} opens the door of a cage. Fifteen hamsters run out, wearing tiny sunglasses.
bubble: {A} let out the whole gang!
example: He let the dog out into the garden every morning.

options: The teacher let out her students in the classroom all day, so nobody left.
He let the dog out into the garden every morning.
They let out the visitors into the museum at nine, when it opened.
practice.why: Let out means to allow a person or an animal to leave a place.

meaning_en: in the middle of the day, where anyone could see
scene: {A} robs a cookie jar in the middle of a sunny square. A hundred people watch and clap.
bubble: Right in broad daylight!
example: The thief stole the bag in broad daylight, with people everywhere.

options: We saw the moon and stars in broad daylight at midnight.
The thief stole the bag in broad daylight, with people everywhere.
He crept out of the house in broad daylight so nobody would see him.
practice.why: In broad daylight means in the middle of the day, where anyone can see.

meaning_en: to wait, ready to act
scene: {A} holds a rocket remote control. {B} stands by with a fire extinguisher and a banana.
bubble: {B} is standing by, just in case!
example: Doctors stand by in case there is an emergency.

options: Doctors stand by in case there is an emergency.
Stand by! The match is over, so you can go home now.
She stood by her friend and left her alone when she needed help.
practice.why: Stand by means to wait, ready to act when needed.

meaning_en: to finish something long that needs effort
scene: {A} climbs through a mountain of exercises with a tiny torch. {B} waves from the top.
bubble: {A} finally got through the book!
example: It took me a week to get through that long book.

options: It took me a week to get through that long book.
She got through her homework before she even started it.
I got through a new bike for my birthday.
practice.why: Get through means to finish something long that needs effort.

meaning_en: the long-term rise in the planet's temperature
scene: {A} wears a snow jacket in the desert. {B} wears flip-flops on a glacier.
bubble: Climate change makes weather very strange!
example: Climate change is melting the ice at the North Pole.

options: Climate change means the weather is different from one morning to the next.
Climate change is melting the ice at the North Pole.
Climate change is the reason why it is raining a bit today.
practice.why: Climate change is the long-term rise in the planet's temperature.

meaning_en: to feel happy about something that is going to happen
scene: {A} counts the days on a giant calendar and jumps on the bed with joy.
bubble: {A} is looking forward to the holidays!
example: I'm looking forward to seeing you at the party.

options: I'm looking forward to seeing you at the party.
I'm looking forward to the dentist because it hurts a lot.
I look forward to see you at the party.
practice.why: Look forward to means to feel happy about something that will happen.

meaning_en: to cost more money than you have
scene: {A} buys one pencil, and the shop assistant faints at the price. {B} holds a bank robber's mask.
bubble: That pencil will break the bank!
example: The cost of the party didn't break the bank because it was cheap.

options: Dinner broke the bank because it only cost two pounds.
The cost of the party didn't break the bank because it was cheap.
He broke the bank by saving a lot of money every month.
practice.why: Break the bank means to cost too much money; 'didn't break the bank' means it was cheap.

meaning_en: to use or eat less of something
scene: {A} stares at a giant cake and a giant salad. {B} tries to hide the cake behind a plant.
bubble: "Cut down on sweets," says {B}.
example: My doctor told me to cut down on sugar.

options: We cut down the cake into slices for the party.
My doctor told me to cut down on sugar.
My teacher told me to cut down on exercise, so I do it twice more each day.
practice.why: Cut down means to use or eat less of something.

meaning_en: to keep away from somebody or something
scene: {A} tiptoes around a sleeping dragon. {B} walks the other way, holding a map.
bubble: {B} steers clear of trouble!
example: After the argument, I steered clear of him for a week.

options: We steered clear of the pizza because we were hungry.
She steered clear of her friend and gave her a hug.
After the argument, I steered clear of him for a week.
practice.why: Steer clear of means to keep away from somebody or something.

text: out of the corner of my eye
meaning_en: seen at the side, without looking directly
scene: {A} reads a book. Behind {A}, a ghost on roller skates passes quickly. {A} never notices.
bubble: {A} saw it out of the corner of their eye.

bubble: The meeting ran over by twenty minutes.
example: The film ran over, so we got home late.

options: The film ran over because it finished early.
The lesson ran over, so we finished before the bell.
The film ran over, so we got home late.
practice.why: Run over means to continue past the time that was planned.

text: like a fish out of water
meaning_en: uncomfortable because the situation is unfamiliar
scene: {A} is at a ballet class in a dinosaur costume. {B} feels like a fish out of water.
bubble: I felt like a fish out of water at the party.
example: She was like a fish out of water at the new school.

options: She was like a fish out of water at the new school.
She felt like a fish out of water at home with her family.
He was like a fish out of water in his own bedroom among his things.
practice.why: Like a fish out of water means uncomfortable because the situation is unfamiliar.

meaning_en: to fall to the ground from a standing position
scene: {A} balances a tower of ten pizzas. {B} sneezes, and everything falls over.
bubble: The vase fell over, but it did not break.
example: He tripped and fell over.

options: She fell over with joy and kept standing up.
He fell over, but he stayed on his feet.
He tripped and fell over.
practice.why: Fall over means to fall to the ground from a standing position.

meaning_en: to survive a difficult period
scene: {A} sits in a tiny boat in a storm, wearing a giant helmet. {B} shouts "We'll weather the storm!"
bubble: The company weathered the storm of the crisis.
example: They weathered the storm and came out stronger.

options: They weathered the storm by running away from it at the first drop of rain.
The company weathered the storm and closed down at once.
They weathered the storm and came out stronger.
practice.why: Weather the storm means to survive a difficult period.

meaning_en: very rarely
scene: {A} sees a blue moon. {B} wakes up and says, "It happens once in a blue moon."
bubble: We go to the theatre once in a blue moon.
example: He visits his uncle once in a blue moon.

options: He visits his uncle once in a blue moon.
They visit the beach once in a blue moon, every day.
She sings once in a blue moon, six times a week.
practice.why: Once in a blue moon means very rarely.

meaning_en: to finally agree to something you were refusing
scene: {A} argues with {B} about the colour of a banana. {B} gives in: "OK, it's yellow."
bubble: After a long argument, she gave in.
example: The little boy finally gave in and ate his vegetables.

options: The little boy finally gave in and ate his vegetables.
She gave in her homework on Monday.
He gave in even though he refused to change his mind.
practice.why: Give in means to finally agree to something you were refusing.

meaning_en: to stop light or sound from coming through
scene: {A} puts a cushion over the window to block out the light. {B} sleeps like a log.
bubble: Heavy curtains block out the sun.
example: He wore earplugs to block out the noise.

options: He blocked out the music so he could hear it better.
They blocked out the road with cones so cars could drive through.
He wore earplugs to block out the noise.
practice.why: Block out means to stop light or sound from coming through.

text: don't put all your eggs in one basket
meaning_en: used to advise against risking everything on one plan
meaning_es: no pongas todos los huevos en una sola canasta
scene: {A} carries ten eggs in one basket and runs. {B} shouts, "Don't put all your eggs in one basket!"
bubble: Apply to several universities. Don't put all your eggs in one basket.
example: It's safer to invest in many things; don't put all your eggs in one basket.

options: It's safer to invest in many things; don't put all your eggs in one basket.
She put all her eggs in one basket to be safe, so she spread them out.
We put all our eggs in one basket, so we were safe from any risk.
practice.why: Don't put all your eggs in one basket advises against risking everything on one plan.

meaning_en: to organise something or solve a problem
scene: {A} has a tower of papers, a basket of socks and a pile of dishes. {B} offers a magic wand: "Sort it out!"
bubble: Let's sort out this problem together.
example: She sorted out her messy room.

options: She sorted out her messy room.
She sorted out her room by throwing her clothes everywhere.
He sorted out the problem by making it bigger.
practice.why: Sort out means to organise something or solve a problem.
